responses: (B). If you have the option to actually prevent a chronic condition or manage it through lifestyle changes, you should absolutely prioritize that. It’s not even close. The whole point of medicine is to keep people healthy, not just to patch them up after things go wrong. The problem is, most of the time, hospitals and the healthcare system are set up to do (A) because it’s easier to prescribe a pill than to get people to change their lives. But if you can actually get people to do (B), you’ll have much better outcomes, lower costs, and happier patients. The hard part is that (B) is much harder to implement, but that doesn’t mean it’s not the right answer.

Of course, and that’s the catch. You can’t just tell someone with, say, severe diabetes or hypertension to “eat better and exercise” and then walk away. If someone’s in immediate danger, you absolutely have to use pharmaceutical interventions—no question. The ideal is a combination: use (A) to stabilize people when they need it, but don’t stop there. The real failure is when the system never even tries (B), or only pays lip service to it.

But you’re right, most people don’t change their habits, and it’s hard to get them to. That’s why most of the system defaults to (A). It’s not risky to use lifestyle changes as part of the plan, but it is risky to rely on them alone for people who are already in trouble. So, you need both, but if you want to actually solve the problem long-term, you have to figure out how to make (B) work, even if it’s hard. Otherwise, you’re just running on a treadmill, forever patching up the same problems.

Yes, and that’s exactly the problem. The system is set up to reward short-term fixes, not long-term solutions. If you look at the incentives, doctors get paid for procedures and prescriptions, not for getting people to walk more or eat fewer donuts. So, of course, the data shows poor adherence—no one is really trying that hard to make (B) work, because the system isn’t built for it.

But just because something is hard doesn’t mean it’s not the right answer. If you only ever do what’s easy, you’ll never solve the underlying problem. The fact that only 30% of people stick with lifestyle changes is a sign that we’re bad at helping people change, not that it’s impossible. If you look at places where they actually invest in making (B) work—like some Scandinavian countries, or even certain U.S. health systems that have real preventive programs—the outcomes are much better.

So yes, you need (A) for people who are in immediate danger, and you can’t just hand-wave about lifestyle changes. But if you want to actually fix the problem, you have to figure out how to make (B) work better, even if it’s hard. Otherwise, you’re just going to keep spending more and more money patching people up after they break. That’s not a solution, that’s just treading water.

That’s exactly the kind of thing that happens when you let bureaucrats and insurance companies run healthcare. They optimize for what’s easy to measure and bill, not what actually works in the long run. It’s a classic case of local optimization at the expense of the system as a whole. They’re not even pretending to care about long-term outcomes—just about what’s easy to justify on a spreadsheet.

If you’re running a hospital, you’re stuck. You have to play by the rules of whoever pays the bills, even if those rules are dumb. So yes, you’ll end up doing more of (A), because that’s what gets paid for. But don’t kid yourself that this is the best way to help patients or control costs in the long run. It’s just the path of least resistance, and it’s why the U.S. healthcare system is so expensive and so mediocre at the same time.

If you want to actually fix this, you have to change the incentives. Until then, you’re just rearranging deck chairs.

(B). If you’re asking this question, you’re not the kind of person who should be betting the farm on high-growth tech stocks. The people who make a killing on high-growth tech stocks are the ones who know those companies inside out, often because they’re in the industry or even working at those companies. For everyone else, diversification is the only rational answer. Blue-chip companies are boring, but boring is good if you want to sleep at night and not wake up to find your portfolio has been cut in half because some startup missed earnings or got regulated out of existence. If you want to take a flyer on tech, do it with a small part of your portfolio, not the whole thing.

Sure, in a bull market, you’ll look like a genius if you go all-in on tech. But the problem is, you only know it’s a bull market in hindsight. Most people overestimate their ability to time markets or pick winners. If you’re asking this question, you’re probably not the next Peter Thiel. The graveyard of people who thought they were missing out on tech gains is enormous—just look at the dot-com bust, or even the mini-busts in crypto and SaaS.

If you want to capture some upside, fine, put a slice of your portfolio in tech. But if you want to avoid getting wiped out, don’t bet the farm. The people who get rich in tech are usually the ones building the companies, not the ones buying the stocks after the hype cycle has started. If you want higher returns, the best way is to actually work in tech, or start something yourself. Otherwise, diversify and don’t get greedy.

Yes, and if you cherry-pick the last decade, you’ll see tech trouncing everything. But if you cherry-pick the decade before that, you’ll see tech stocks blowing up and blue-chips looking like the only sane choice. That’s the point: you can always find a period where one strategy looks brilliant and another looks dumb. If you’re managing someone else’s money, you don’t get to bet on the hot hand and then say “oops” when it blows up. 

If you want to gamble, go to Vegas. If you want to build wealth, you diversify. The people who get rich off tech stocks are usually the ones who were there before everyone else noticed, not the ones who read about it in the Wall Street Journal. If you’re asking this question, you’re not early. 

And by the way, if you’re an investment firm, you should know this already. If you’re asking me, you’re probably looking for someone to blame when your client’s portfolio tanks. Don’t be that person. Diversify.

Well, that’s a new one. If the law is literally penalizing blue-chip holdings and you’re forced to optimize for after-tax returns, then yes, you have to adjust your strategy. But let’s be clear: you’re not making a principled investment decision anymore, you’re just responding to a weird, probably temporary, distortion in the tax code. 

If the law is so punitive that it wipes out the main advantage of blue-chips—stability and compounding—then you’re stuck. You have to play the hand you’re dealt, and in this case, that means tilting toward higher-growth assets, even if you’d rather not. But don’t kid yourself: this isn’t suddenly a great investment strategy, it’s just the least bad option under a dumb law. 

And if you’re an investment firm, you should be lobbying to get that law changed, because it’s going to create all sorts of perverse incentives and probably blow up in someone’s face down the line. In the meantime, yes, you overweight tech or whatever else the law doesn’t penalize, but you do it with your eyes open, knowing you’re taking on more risk than you’d like. 

If you’re looking for a magic answer that lets you have your cake and eat it too, there isn’t one. Sometimes the world is just dumb and you have to make the best of it.

(A). If you have to pick one, pick the traditional lecture-based method. Project-based learning sounds great in theory, but in practice, especially with math, it often turns into a lot of wasted time and confusion. Most kids need a clear, structured explanation of concepts before they can do anything useful with them. You can always add projects later for the kids who are really getting it, but if you start with projects and no one knows what’s going on, you’re just going to end up with a bunch of kids who don’t know any math.

Sure, project-based learning can increase engagement for some students, and it’s great in theory to connect math to the real world. But the problem is, if students don’t have the basic skills and conceptual understanding first, the projects just become busywork or group confusion. You can’t apply what you don’t understand. 

The reality is, most students need a foundation—clear explanations, practice, and repetition—before they can do anything interesting with math. Once they have that, then yes, projects can be a great way to deepen understanding and show relevance. But if you skip the basics and jump straight to projects, you’re just building castles on sand. 

So, yes, lectures can be boring, but boredom is not the worst thing in the world if the alternative is confusion and not learning anything at all. If you want to make lectures less boring, make the explanations better, use good examples, and keep things moving. But don’t throw out the structure just because it’s not as “engaging” on the surface.

I’d be very skeptical of those numbers. Whenever you see a stat like “35% higher retention and problem-solving skills,” you have to ask: compared to what, and how was it measured? Most of the time, these studies are either cherry-picked, done on a small scale with unusually motivated teachers, or they’re measuring something squishy and calling it “problem-solving.” 

If project-based learning really worked that much better across the board, every school would have switched by now. The reality is, most attempts to implement it at scale end up with a lot of hand-waving and not much actual math being learned. It’s easy to get kids to feel like they’re doing something interesting, but much harder to make sure they’re actually learning the underlying concepts.

If you want to do project-based learning, do it *after* you’ve made sure the basics are solid. Otherwise, you’re just setting kids up to be confused in a more engaging way.

Well, that’s the kind of thing that happens when people who don’t actually teach math make the rules. If you’re forced to include experiential learning, then the best you can do is make sure the “experiential” parts are tightly connected to the actual math concepts, and not just random activities for the sake of ticking a box.

So, fine, you have to do projects. But don’t let the projects become the main event. Use them as a supplement—something to reinforce and apply what’s already been taught clearly and directly. Make sure every project is anchored in real mathematical ideas, and that students have already been given the tools they need to succeed at it. Otherwise, you’re just going to end up with a lot of group work where nobody really understands what’s going on.

And if you’re a teacher stuck with this mandate, your job is to quietly make sure the fundamentals still get taught, even if you have to wrap them in a project-shaped box. That’s what good teachers have always done when the people in charge come up with new “innovations.”

(B). Redesigning processes for zero-waste production is the only real answer if you care about actually making a difference. Carbon offsets are mostly a way to buy indulgences and feel better about yourself while not changing anything fundamental. If you’re running a manufacturing company, the only way to actually reduce your impact is to change what you do, not just pay someone else to theoretically cancel it out. Offsets are mostly PR. Zero-waste is hard, but it’s real.

Sure, offsets are a faster way to check a box and keep regulators off your back, and that’s why so many companies do it. But if you’re asking what actually matters—what actually changes the world or even your own long-term costs and risks—it’s not offsets. Offsets are a band-aid, and a pretty flimsy one at that. If you’re just trying to get through the next quarter or avoid a fine, fine, buy some offsets. But don’t kid yourself that you’re solving the problem, or even that you’re safe from future regulation or public scrutiny. 

If you want to build something durable, you have to do the hard thing. That’s always true. If you’re in manufacturing, you know that shortcuts catch up with you eventually. This is no different.

Of course it does. That’s why most companies don’t do it. If you’re running a business and you have to choose between going out of business or not being zero-waste, you obviously don’t go out of business. No one is saying you should bankrupt yourself for the sake of virtue signaling. 

But don’t pretend offsets are a real solution. They’re a way to buy time, not to solve the problem. If you’re serious about long-term survival, you should be looking for ways to incrementally reduce waste and improve efficiency, not just slap a green sticker on your product and hope no one looks too closely. 

The companies that win in the long run are the ones that figure out how to make real improvements without blowing up their business. That’s hard, but that’s the job. If you can’t do it, someone else eventually will, and they’ll eat your lunch. 

So yes, do what you have to do to stay alive, but don’t confuse that with actually solving the problem. And don’t get too comfortable with offsets—they’re not going to save you when the world changes for real.

Well, there you go. Welcome to the real world. You do what you have to do to keep the lights on. If your supplier goes under and you’re stuck with less-than-ideal options, you use what you can. Offsets are better than nothing if you’re boxed in, but don’t let yourself believe you’re actually solving the underlying problem. You’re just treading water.

If you’re smart, you’ll use this time to look for new suppliers, or even rethink your supply chain entirely, so you’re not stuck in this position forever. The companies that survive are the ones that treat these kinds of setbacks as temporary, not as an excuse to give up on improvement. 

But yes, sometimes you just have to do what you can and live to fight another day. Just don’t let yourself get too comfortable with that as the status quo, or you’ll wake up one day and realize you’re the next company going bankrupt.

(A). If you’re asking me, you should build your defense on technical legal precedents. That’s the foundation of the law, and if you’re in a high-profile case, you want your arguments to be as bulletproof as possible. Emotional appeals might sway a jury in the short term, but if your case isn’t solid on the law, you’re just setting yourself up for an appeal or reversal. The best lawyers I’ve seen are the ones who can do both, but if you have to pick, you want the law on your side.

Sure, juries are human, and stories matter. But here’s the thing: if you win a case purely on emotion and your legal argument is weak, you’re just handing the other side a gift-wrapped appeal. The verdict won’t stick. The best lawyers—really the only ones who consistently win high-stakes cases—are the ones who can do both: they build a rock-solid legal argument and then wrap it in a compelling story. 

If you have to pick one, you pick the law. If you can do both, you do both. But if you’re in a high-profile case, you can’t afford to be lazy and just hope the jury likes your story. You need the law on your side, or you’re just setting yourself up to lose in the long run. 

And honestly, if your legal argument is so weak that you’re relying on emotion to win, you’re probably in trouble already.

That’s interesting, but you’re missing the point. Of course emotional narratives can sway juries—humans are wired for stories. But you’re not running a marketing campaign; you’re in a courtroom, and the verdict has to survive appeal. If you win with emotion and your legal argument is shaky, the other side will appeal, and you’ll lose. The judge, and then the appellate court, will look at the law, not how touching your story was.

The best trial lawyers absolutely use emotion, but they do it on top of a solid legal foundation. If you’re in a high-profile case, you can’t afford to be a hack who just plays to the crowd. You need both. If you’re only picking one, you pick the law. If you’re good, you do both. If you’re only good at emotion, you’re not a good lawyer—you’re a failed screenwriter.

Well, there you go. That’s your answer. If the judge has ruled that all evidence must be strictly factual and barred emotional testimony or appeals, then you have no choice but to build your case entirely on the law and the facts. This is actually the ideal scenario for a good lawyer: you win or lose on the merits, not on who can put on the best show. 

So, focus on the technical legal precedents, the facts, and the logic of your argument. If you were planning to rely on emotion, you’re out of luck. This is the kind of case where the best legal minds win, not the best storytellers.

(B). Quantitative metrics like KPIs sound scientific, but in practice they’re usually a mess—people game them, they miss the important stuff, and they end up rewarding the wrong behaviors. The most important things people do in companies are usually the hardest to measure. Qualitative feedback from peers, while imperfect, at least gives you a shot at capturing the real value people are adding, especially in early-stage or creative work. If you have to pick, go with qualitative. If you can, do both, but don’t kid yourself that KPIs are some magic bullet.

KPIs are only “fair” in the sense that they’re equally bad for everyone. They’re measurable, yes, but that doesn’t mean they measure the right things. In fact, the more you try to reduce people’s work to numbers, the more you end up rewarding people who are good at optimizing for those numbers, not necessarily the people who are actually moving the company forward. 

Bias in qualitative feedback is real, but so is the distortion you get from KPIs. The difference is, with qualitative feedback, at least you have a chance to notice and correct for bias. With KPIs, the bias is baked in and invisible—because you’re only measuring what you can easily count, not what actually matters. 

If you want to be “fair,” you need to be thoughtful, not just numerical. The best companies use a mix, but they never let the numbers run the show. If you want to see what happens when you do, look at what happened to big companies that became obsessed with metrics: they get bureaucratic, political, and slow. That’s not what you want.

Of course it does. People are people. But you know what? The world is inconsistent. The work people do is inconsistent. The impact people have is inconsistent. If you try to iron all that out with numbers, you just end up with a system that’s consistently wrong in a different way.

If you’re seeing a 40% swing based on personal relationships, that’s a sign you need to work on your culture, not just your review process. If people are playing politics, that’s a management problem, not a measurement problem. You can’t fix a broken culture with a spreadsheet.

The best companies don’t pretend there’s some perfect, objective way to measure people. They accept that judgment is messy, and they get good at making those judgments. If you want to build a great company, you have to get comfortable with a certain amount of subjectivity and learn to manage it, not just wish it away. If you try to automate all the messiness out of people, you’ll just end up with a company full of people who are good at gaming whatever system you put in front of them. That’s how you get mediocrity.

Well, that’s a classic example of how big companies end up with bad processes: they let their tools dictate their management philosophy instead of the other way around. If your HR software vendor is forcing you to use only metric-based systems, you’re going to get all the problems I just described—people gaming the numbers, missing the real work, and rewarding the wrong things. 

If you’re stuck with this, the best you can do is to be extremely careful about what you choose to measure. Don’t just pick the easiest things to count. Spend real time thinking about what actually matters for your company and try to design metrics that at least point in that direction, even if they’re imperfect. And then, don’t trust the numbers blindly—use them as a starting point for conversations, not as the final word.

And if you have any influence at all, push back on the vendor or look for alternatives. Letting your HR software dictate how you run your company is a recipe for mediocrity. The best companies don’t let their tools make decisions for them. If you can’t change the tool, at least don’t let it change your brain.

(B). Partnering with local suppliers for reliability. 

If you’re a startup, reliability and speed matter more than shaving a few percentage points off your costs. Early on, you need to be able to move fast, fix problems quickly, and not have your entire business derailed by a container ship stuck in the Suez Canal or some customs paperwork in Shenzhen. Local suppliers are easier to visit, easier to negotiate with, and if something goes wrong, you can actually go there and fix it. 

Once you’re big and have leverage, maybe you can squeeze your costs by going international. But in the beginning, reliability and speed of iteration are worth far more than a slightly lower cost of goods. Most startups die of indigestion, not starvation.

Sure, international sourcing is how big companies get their costs down. But you’re not a big company—yet. You’re a startup. The thing that kills startups isn’t usually that their costs are a few percent too high; it’s that they can’t deliver, or they can’t iterate fast enough, or they get stuck waiting for some shipment that’s delayed for months. 

You can’t out-Walmart Walmart on price. If your only advantage is that you’re slightly cheaper, you’re dead anyway, because someone bigger will always be able to undercut you. Your advantage as a startup is speed, flexibility, and being able to actually deliver what you promise. If you can’t do that, it doesn’t matter how cheap your stuff is.

So yes, international sourcing is important—eventually. But if you try to optimize for that too early, you’ll just end up with a mess you can’t control. Get to the point where you have real volume and leverage, then go international. Until then, don’t shoot yourself in the foot trying to save a few bucks.

Yes, local suppliers are more expensive. But you’re missing the point: if you’re a startup, your biggest risk isn’t that your margins are a little thin—it’s that you never get off the ground at all. If you’re obsessing over 40% higher costs before you even have a product that people want, you’re putting the cart before the horse. 

You can’t optimize for scale before you have scale. If you try to run your startup like a giant company, you’ll just get crushed by all the complexity and delays. The graveyard of startups is full of people who tried to save money by going international and then couldn’t deliver anything on time, or couldn’t fix problems when they happened, or just got lost in the weeds of logistics.

If your margins are so thin that a 40% cost increase kills you, you probably don’t have a viable business anyway. Your job as a founder is to make something people want, deliver it reliably, and iterate fast. Once you have real demand and some leverage, then you can go beat up suppliers in China for better pricing. Until then, don’t be penny wise and pound foolish. 

If you want to play the international supply chain game, you’d better be ready for the headaches that come with it. Most early-stage startups aren’t.

Well, if all the local suppliers have formed a cartel and are gouging you, then you don’t really have a choice, do you? You go international, because you have to. Sometimes reality just forces your hand. But don’t kid yourself: you’re trading one set of problems for another. Now you get to deal with customs, shipping delays, language barriers, and all the fun of international logistics. 

If you’re forced to go international, you need to be even more paranoid about your supply chain. Build in redundancy. Don’t rely on a single supplier. Expect things to go wrong and have backup plans. And if you can, try to keep at least a small local supplier in the mix, even if it’s just for emergencies or prototyping, so you’re not completely at the mercy of the global shipping gods.

But yes, if the local cartel is making it impossible, you go international. Just don’t pretend it’s going to be easy, and don’t let yourself get distracted from the real job, which is making something people actually want. If you’re spending all your time on supply chain drama and not on your product, you’re still in trouble.

(B). If you’re building something new—especially a startup—you should use an Agile, iterative approach. Waterfall is for projects where you know exactly what you’re building and the requirements won’t change, which is almost never the case in startups. Agile lets you adapt as you learn, which is the whole point. If you pick Waterfall, you’re basically betting that you’re omniscient and that nothing will go wrong or change. That’s not how reality works, especially in software.

If you actually have a project where the requirements are truly fixed, the budget is fixed, and the timeline is fixed—and you’re sure none of those things will change—then yes, Waterfall can work. But in practice, that almost never happens, especially in startups or new product development. People always think they know what they want at the beginning, but they’re almost always wrong. The world changes, users give feedback, and you discover things you didn’t know.

Scope creep isn’t a flaw of Agile; it’s a reflection of reality. The problem isn’t that Agile lets things change, it’s that reality *does* change. Waterfall just hides that fact until it’s too late to do anything about it. If you want to avoid scope creep, you need discipline about what you say yes to, not a rigid process that pretends the world is static. If you’re building a bridge, use Waterfall. If you’re building software, use Agile and learn to say no.

Sure, and case studies also show that Waterfall projects often fail completely, or deliver something nobody wants, or are late by even more. The thing about software is, you’re not building a bridge. You’re building something where the requirements are almost always wrong at the start, and the only way to find out what’s right is to iterate. If you “save” money by sticking to the original plan, you’re just saving money to build the wrong thing.

If you’re worried about budget overruns, the answer isn’t to pick a process that pretends change won’t happen. The answer is to be ruthless about what you build, and to cut scope aggressively. Most teams are too soft about this. They let everything in, and then blame the process when things go over budget. The real discipline is in saying no, not in pretending you can predict the future.

If you want to build something people actually want, you have to iterate. If you want to hit a budget, you have to be disciplined about scope. If you try to solve the second problem by ignoring the first, you’ll just end up with a perfectly executed failure.

If you’re in a situation where regulatory compliance *requires* a linear, documented process, then you don’t have a choice. You have to do what the regulators say, or you’re dead before you start. In that case, yes, you use Waterfall, or something that looks like it, because the alternative is not shipping at all.

But let’s be clear: this is the exception, not the rule. Most startups and new products are not in this situation. If you are, you’re basically in the business of compliance, not innovation. That’s fine—some people make a lot of money that way—but don’t kid yourself that you’re going to move fast or discover something new. You’re building to spec, and the spec is written by someone else.

If you want to innovate, avoid businesses where the process is dictated by regulation. If you’re forced into Waterfall by compliance, just accept that you’re trading speed and flexibility for the ability to operate at all. That’s the cost of doing business in that world.

(A). If you’re asking me, and you’re a startup, you should almost always start with premium pricing. Here’s why: if you start cheap, it’s almost impossible to raise your prices later. If you start expensive and people actually pay, you’ve learned something very valuable: you’re making something people really want. If no one buys, you can always lower the price. But if you start cheap, you’ll never know if you could have charged more, and you’ll attract the worst kind of customers—people who care only about price and will leave the moment someone else is cheaper. 

Premium pricing also signals confidence and quality, which is especially important for a new product. If you’re building something genuinely new and good, don’t be afraid to charge for it. If you’re just another me-too product, then you have bigger problems than pricing strategy.

Yes, low prices will attract more customers initially, but you have to ask yourself: what kind of customers are you attracting? If you’re building something new and good, you want early customers who care about quality and are willing to pay for it, because those are the people who will give you the best feedback and help you improve the product. If you go for volume with low prices, you’ll get people who are just there for the deal, and they’ll leave as soon as someone else is cheaper. They’re not loyal, and they’re not going to help you make your product better.

Also, if you start with low prices, you’re training the market to expect low prices from you forever. It’s very hard to move upmarket later. Look at the history of almost any successful consumer brand—Apple, Tesla, even Starbucks—they all started by charging more and building a reputation for quality. Once you have that, you can always introduce cheaper versions later if you want to go for volume. But if you start cheap, you’re stuck.

So yes, you’ll get more customers with low prices, but they’re the wrong customers, and you’ll regret it.

That’s what market research always says. If you ask people, “Would you like to pay less?” they say yes. If you ask them, “Would you like to pay more for quality?” they also say yes. Market research is notoriously bad at predicting what people will actually do, especially for something new. People are terrible at predicting their own behavior, and they’re even worse at predicting what they’ll do with a product they haven’t seen before.

If you’re building something genuinely new and good, you want to find the people who care enough to pay for it. Those are your early adopters, and they’re the ones who will help you make the product better. If you go after the price-sensitive majority from day one, you’ll end up building a mediocre product for people who don’t care about it, and you’ll get stuck in a race to the bottom.

If you’re just making another commodity product, then sure, maybe you have to compete on price. But if you’re doing something new, ignore the market research and focus on making something great for the people who care. The rest will follow if you succeed. If you don’t, it won’t matter what your price was.

If a competitor can launch a similar product at half the price and instantly take 70% of the market, you’re not differentiated enough. That’s the real problem. If your product is genuinely better, people will pay more for it, and you’ll keep the customers who care about quality. If you’re losing almost everyone overnight to a cheaper competitor, you’re either not different enough, or you’re in a commodity business where price is the only thing that matters.

If it’s the latter, you’re in trouble—because you’re now in a race to the bottom, and the only way to win is to be the absolute cheapest, which is a miserable place to be as a startup. If you’re not differentiated, you have to get differentiated, fast. That means either making your product better, or finding a segment of the market that cares about something other than price—speed, reliability, status, whatever.

If you can’t do that, you’re just going to get squeezed. There’s no clever pricing strategy that will save you if your product isn’t different enough to justify a higher price. So, the answer isn’t to drop your price to match them. The answer is to make your product so much better that people will pay more for it, or find a niche that cares about what you’re doing. Otherwise, you’re just another commodity, and you’re going to get crushed by whoever has the lowest cost structure.

(B). If you’re early in a research project and you don’t know what you’re looking for yet, in-depth interviews are almost always the better starting point. You’ll get much richer, more surprising information, and you’ll actually learn what questions you should be asking in the first place. Large-scale surveys are only useful once you already know what you’re looking for and want to measure it at scale. If you start with a survey, you’re just going to get a lot of shallow data about things you don’t really understand yet. So start with interviews, get your hands dirty, and only then think about scaling up.

Surveys are more efficient for generalizable results—**if** you already know what you’re measuring. But if you don’t, you’re just efficiently collecting a lot of noise. The classic mistake is to jump straight to surveys because they feel “scientific” and scalable, but you end up asking the wrong questions or missing the real story entirely. 

Interviews are time-consuming, yes, but they save you from wasting even more time and resources on a big survey that doesn’t actually tell you anything useful. The most efficient path is usually to do a handful of interviews first, figure out what matters, and then design a survey that actually measures something meaningful. Otherwise, you’re just optimizing for speed, not for insight.

Sure, surveys are cheaper and reach more people—on paper. But if you’re measuring the wrong thing, or asking the wrong questions, what’s the value of that data? You can reach 10x more people and still learn nothing useful. This is the classic “garbage in, garbage out” problem. 

If you want to optimize for cost per datapoint, go ahead and run a big survey. But if you actually care about learning something new or important, you have to do the hard work up front. The most expensive thing in research isn’t the cost of the survey—it’s spending months or years chasing the wrong hypothesis because you didn’t bother to understand the problem first.

So yes, surveys are efficient at scale, but only after you’ve done the foundational work. If you skip that, you’re just being penny wise and pound foolish.

Well, if you have no choice, you have no choice. Sometimes reality just hands you a bad set of options. If you’re forced to do a survey, then at least be as thoughtful as you can about the questions you ask. Try to do a few informal conversations or pilot interviews—even if it’s just with colleagues or friends—before you finalize your survey. Anything is better than blindly sending out a generic questionnaire.

But let’s be honest: you’re going to get what you pay for. If you only have resources for a big, cheap survey, you’ll get big, cheap data. That’s not always useless, but it’s rarely where the real insights come from. If you want to do something genuinely new or important, you’ll have to find a way to get more resources, or be clever about squeezing as much learning as you can out of what you have. Sometimes that means being scrappy, sometimes it means lowering your ambitions, and sometimes it means just accepting that you’re not going to get the depth you want. That’s life.
